results.header: Out of the Cellar: Spatio-temporal Signatures of Rat Sightings in Chicago | Urban Ecosystems | Springer Nature Link Skip to main content Advertisement Log in Menu Find a journal Publish with us Track your research Search Saved research Cart Home Urban Ecosystems Article Out of the Cellar: Spatio-temporal Signatures of Rat Sightings in Chicago Research Published: 07 November 2026 Volume 29 , article number 308 ( 2026 ) Cite this article Save article View saved research Urban Ecosystems Aims and scope Submit manuscript Edward Helderop 1 & Tony H. Grubesic 1 Abstract Urban rat infestations represent a persistent public health challenge, yet municipal pest management programs often operate reactively and with limited resources. This study applies a suite of spatiotemporal statistical approaches (geographically weighted regression, spatial lag modeling, Random Forest, and Extreme Gradient Boosting) to predict the spatial distribution of rat sightings across Chicago, Illinois, over a fifteen-year observation window (2011–2025). Using 311 service request data linked to a hexagonal grid (150 m cells) and a set of environmental, demographic, and property-value predictors, we assess the individual and ensemble performance of these models on held-out 2025 rat-sighting data. Our comparative analysis demonstrates that the machine learning frameworks and the spatial lag model generally outperformed geographically weighted regression. Specifically, Random Forest, the spatial lag model, and XGBoost each explained approximately 72% of the variance in rat sighting counts, while the ensemble model achieved the highest overall R 2 (0.73). Variable importance analysis identified recent historical sighting counts as the dominant positive predictor, followed by food establishment density and vacant property rates (both positively associated), and median household income and property values (negatively associated). Spatial hotspot analysis revealed that persistent rat activity hotspots were concentrated in high-density mixed-use corridors characterized by dense commercial food clusters, connected public alleyway infrastructure, and older residential housing stock with elevated vacancy rates. These findings suggest that proactive, data-driven approaches can identify areas in need of resource targeting to create more efficient interventions for cities facing chronic urban rodent challenges. This study aimed to quantify aboveground biomass, carbon stocks, and their illustrative economic valuation in an urban Tiny Forest located in southeastern Brazil. A complete tree inventory was conducted across a 2.76-ha area, including all living trees with a diameter at breast height (DBH) ≥ 5 cm. Aboveground biomass was estimated using an allometric equation developed for urban trees, carbon stocks were calculated using a conversion factor of 0.47, and an illustrative economic valuation was derived from a reference price in the voluntary carbon market. The inventory recorded 539 trees belonging to 68 species and 24 botanical families, with native species accounting for 79.0% of the individuals. Total aboveground biomass was estimated at 95.09 Mg (34.45 Mg ha⁻¹), corresponding to 44.69 Mg of carbon (16.19 Mg C ha⁻¹) and 163.88 Mg CO₂e. The illustrative economic valuation of the stored carbon was US$3,349.64. Native species accounted for 86.46% of the estimated carbon stock, with Moquilea tomentosa and Handroanthus impetiginosus among the main contributors. Carbon storage varied with species composition and tree structural characteristics, indicating that abundance alone does not determine species contributions to carbon stocks. These findings demonstrate that small urban forest remnants can represent measurable carbon reservoirs and provide local-scale information to support urban green infrastructure planning. However, the estimates represent carbon stocks at a single point in time and do not establish carbon sequestration rates or potential revenue from certified carbon credits. results.header: Global urban tree leaf area under climate change: divergent projected trajectories and the limits of space-for-time inference | Urban Ecosystems | Springer Nature Link Skip to main content Advertisement Log in Menu Find a journal Publish with us Track your research Search Saved research Cart Home Urban Ecosystems Article Global urban tree leaf area under climate change: divergent projected trajectories and the limits of space-for-time inference Research Open access Published: 06 November 2026 Volume 29 , article number 306 ( 2026 ) Cite this article You have full access to this open access article Download PDF Save article View saved research Urban Ecosystems Aims and scope Submit manuscript Global urban tree leaf area under climate change: divergent projected trajectories and the limits of space-for-time inference Download PDF Gianmarco Goycochea Casas ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0001-5491-8771 1 52 Accesses Explore all metrics Abstract Urban trees moderate city climates, yet how their leaf-area density relates to projected future climates is poorly constrained globally. We fitted a Random Forest model to monthly temperature and precipitation normals and the multi-year mean leaf area index (LAI) derived from a satellite-informed machine-learning urban tree product across 21,590 urban cells, then projected end-of-century change under six Shared Socioeconomic Pathways. Leave-one-continent-out validation gave \(R^2 = 0.846\) (95% CI \(0.813\) – \(0.873\) from spatial-block resampling), but that spatial skill does not transfer to time: driven by observed reanalysis anomalies over exactly the satellite record, the same relationship reproduces neither the magnitude nor the pattern of observed change ( \(\rho = +0.087\) ). The response variable is itself a machine-learning product built from overlapping climate predictors, so the spatial fit is not independent evidence of that relationship either. Under modified Mann–Kendall tests with false-discovery-rate control, 19.8% of cells greened and 5.3% browned during 2000–2022, roughly half the browning obtained without those corrections. Global mean change is positive under all scenarios, yet 32.6% of cells decline under SSP5-8.5, with declines concentrated in tropical humid cities and gains at high latitudes. Two further results bound them: 10.6% of cells fall outside the fitted climate domain under SSP5-8.5, and four algorithms agree on the sign of change at only 68.1% of cells. We report these as changes implied by transferring a spatial relationship into future climates, not forecasts: the zonal contrast is the most reproducible result across the evaluated algorithms; cell-level magnitudes and city orderings are not. Urban heat islands raise air temperatures in built environments well above their rural surroundings (Santamouris 2020 ), and urban trees are among the few interventions that address several of the resulting problems at once, moderating surface and air temperature, intercepting rainfall, sequestering carbon and improving amenity (Bowler et al. 2010 ; Livesley et al. 2016 ; Endreny et al. 2017 ; Turner-Skoff and Cavender 2019 ; Schwaab et al. 202 ), and the magnitude of the cooling benefit has grown measurably over the satellite era (Zhao et al. 2023 ). Murphy ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-7670-2469 1 , Peter A. Nelson 2 , Mary Powell 3 & … Josh Gilbert 4 Show authors 13 Accesses Explore all metrics Abstract Urban riverscapes contribute substantially to the ecological function, livability, and sustainability of urban and suburban environments, yet their conservation and restoration require assessment approaches that capture interacting ecological, hydrologic, geomorphic, and social dimensions across spatial scales. This article presents URBAN—the Urban Riverscape conditions-Based Assessment for management Needs—as a flexible method for implementing the Technical Domain of the Urban Riverscapes Assessment Framework. URBAN is distinctive in explicitly linking Human Connections and Values with physical processes, community priorities, and anthropogenic stressors that shape long-term riverscape recovery. The assessment is organized around four Facets: Human Connections and Values, Hydrologic Processes and Hydraulic Characteristics, Geomorphic Forms and Processes, and Ecological Structure and Processes. Applied in metropolitan Denver, Colorado, USA, URBAN integrates geospatial analysis, rapid field observations, reach typing, response-potential analysis, and scoring criteria to identify stressors, functional conditions, and management-relevant outcomes. Results from the Denver application indicate that functional conditions and community values may align, diverge, or conflict across reaches, underscoring the need for synthesis across Metrics, Indicators, and Facets rather than reliance on isolated measures. In combination with GIS tools and the broader Urban Riverscape Framework, URBAN provides an objective, multi-scale approach for interpreting multi-causal mechanisms, prioritizing preservation and restoration actions, and supporting planning, regulatory, and engagement needs. The Denver case study demonstrates the utility of URBAN for watershed-scale planning, reach-scale prioritization, and transparent communication among managers, practitioners, and communities, while maintaining adaptability to local context and data availability. Ekwemuka 2 , Deborah Bawa 1 , Monday Christopher 1 , Amobi Anselem Chinweike 1 , Onoja Peter Oche 1 , Faith Jesutofunmi Jeremiah 1 , Ukabiala Maduabuchi Ekeoma 3 & … Unique N. Keke 1 Show authors 9 Accesses 1 Altmetric Explore all metrics Abstract Urban expansion is changing bird assemblages across sub-Saharan Africa, where the sorting of species along urban–rural gradients is understudied. We present a multi-scale analysis of bird assemblages at four locations in Minna, central Nigeria, combining trait-environment modelling, ordination, beta-diversity analysis and machine learning. We recorded 115 species (15 orders, 50 families) in 71 single-visit, 10-minute, fixed-radius point counts (April to July 2021). Because locations were sampled at different times, location and season are partly confounded. Bird detection was weakly predicted (AUC = 0.676): generalists and frugivorous birds were more likely to be detected at multiple stations compared to specialists. Abundance where detected was weakly predicted (R² = 0.133) and higher among seed-eating species. Trait-environment interactions did not improve prediction, indicating trait-associated detection rather than trait-mediated environmental filtering. No community metric was predictable at a withheld location, and no feeding-guild model had predictive skill. Composition differed among locations (PERMANOVA pseudo-F = 1.68, R² = 0.070, p = 0.001), although dispersion also differed and the three locations surveyed within nine days did not differ significantly. Beta-diversity was mostly explained by replacement (0.65) compared to nestedness (0.07). Shannon diversity and functional dispersion were lowest in Gidan Kwano, whereas richness did not differ, even after rarefaction. Composition was associated with tree density, tree size, and elevation, yet not independent from geographic distance. Turnover-driven replacement suggests that networks of habitat patches would provide better protection of regional diversity, which should be confirmed through repeated surveys at same seasons. Hamer ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0001-6031-7841 2 , 3 , Zoltán Soltész ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0003-3423-9258 4 , Thu-Hương Huỳnh ORCID: orcid.org/0009-0005-7524-205X 2 , 3 , Ádám Mészáros ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0001-5679-3167 2 , 5 & … Zsófia Horváth ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0003-2857-1094 2 , 3 Show authors 325 Accesses 1 Altmetric Explore all metrics Abstract Mosquitoes in urban environments are considered unpleasant by citizens, and they can represent serious health risks as vectors of pathogens. Invasive Aedes species are continuously spreading in Europe and have been increasingly reported from urban settlements. Some of these mosquito species have been associated with small artificial habitats. Therefore, their presence may also be expected in small plastic garden ponds, which are numerous in urban settings across many parts of Europe. Here, we aimed to determine whether urban waters host a high abundance of mosquitoes and to identify the potential abiotic, biotic and landscape drivers of mosquito presence and abundance in urban ponds. We sampled 93 urban ponds in the city of Budapest (Hungary), comprising 40 garden ponds and 53 other urban ponds of both natural and anthropogenic origin, across highly urbanised areas and suburban areas with a high green index. We collected data on macroinvertebrate communities, pond management, physico-chemical parameters, and pond characteristics (mainly morphology and vegetation cover) measured in situ . Two different mosquito detection techniques were used: dip-net sampling and environmental DNA (eDNA). While only one invasive species ( Aedes koreicus ) was detected, occurring in two ponds, several other species were present, including potential malaria vectors increasingly reported from urban environments: members of the Anopheles maculipennis complex, An. claviger and An. plumbeus . The presence and abundance of mosquitoes was negatively associated with fish presence, regardless of pond type. Contrary to expectations, urbanisation did not play a major role in explaining mosquito presence or abundance in the sampled ponds. These results highlight the importance of local pond characteristics, and particularly the association between fish presence and mosquito occurrence and abundance although the broader ecological effects of fish on pond communities should also be considered. Environmental Geography Biodiversity Freshwater and Marine Ecology Urban Ecology Ecology Environmental Impact Ecological Management of Mosquito Populations Introduction Urbanisation leads to changes in biodiversity mainly through land use and land cover changes, which reduce both species richness and evenness for most biotic communities (Grimm et al. 2008 ). Green and blue spaces in urban areas (e.g. parks, forests, rivers and ponds) can buffer the negative impact of urbanisation on biodiversity (Hyseni et al. 2021 ). Blue infrastructure (i.e., rivers, streams, canals and ponds) provides essential services and benefits for the urban population (Haase et al. 2014 ) as well as supporting freshwater biodiversity (Ferzoco and McCauley 2024 ). Ponds are abundant in urban landscapes in many regions, although they are rarely of natural origin (Horváth et al. 2025 ). These ecosystems often have poor water quality due to pollution and may support exotic species (Oertli and Parris 2019 ). Among other negative consequences for biodiversity, urbanisation both fragments the landscape and creates barriers to organisms’ dispersal, which is key for the assemblage of aquatic communities (Hamer and McDonnell 2008 ; Sanderson et al. 2005 ). Arévalo-Ayala ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0001-6250-6400 5 , 6 Show authors 324 Accesses 1 Altmetric Explore all metrics Abstract Wildlife roadkill represents a major direct threat to many species, affecting population dynamics, and in some cases driving species toward extinction. Although roadkill has been widely documented in Colombia, studies in the Caribbean Region, which encompasses key vulnerable ecosystems such as the Tropical Dry Forest (TDF), remain scarce. Here, we assessed whether road characteristics influence the taxonomic composition of vertebrate roadkill on peri-urban roads in the department of Córdoba. We conducted systematic bicycle surveys along three inter-municipal roads over a three-month period during the dry-to-wet transition season, recording species identity and local road characteristics, including artificial lighting near houses, fences, water bodies, traffic signals, and wildlife crossings. We recorded 317 roadkill events, most of which were identified to species (217), with reptiles representing the largest proportion of records, followed by amphibians, mammals, and birds. The taxonomic composition of roadkill records was associated with local road characteristics. Mammal records were more likely on illuminated road sections and in the absence of fences, but less likely near water bodies. Bird records were less likely in the absence of fences and in the presence of wildlife crossings. Amphibian records were more likely in the presence of pole fences and less likely on illuminated road sections, whereas reptile records were more likely near water bodies. These findings indicate that local road characteristics shape the relative representation of vertebrate groups among roadkill records in peri-urban TDF landscapes. Mitigation measures are necessary to reduce mortality and preserve ecosystem functionality. Similar content being viewed by others Phew! Ethology Mammalogy Primatology Biodiversity Tropical Ecology Animal Geography Wildlife Mortality and Road Ecology Impact Assessment Introduction Roads are one of the main drivers of habitat fragmentation and biodiversity loss in terrestrial ecosystems (Forman and Alexander 1998 ; Fahrig and Rytwinski 2009 ). Wildlife roadkill, in particular, poses a direct threat to numerous species, affecting population dynamics, movement patterns, and reproduction, and in some cases driving species from local to regional extinctions (Laurance et al. 2009 ; Teixeira et al. 2013 ; Grilo et al. 2021 ). Although this issue has been widely documented in Latin American countries such as Brazil, Mexico, and Costa Rica, evidence in Colombia remains limited and taxonomically uneven (Angarita-Corzo et al. 2023 ; Sukhontapatipak et al. 2025 ). Studies in the Colombian Caribbean have reported high rates of roadkill along roads bordering tropical dry forest (TDF) remnants, which are areas of high biodiversity (Monroy et al. 2015 ; Adárraga-Caballero et al. 2019 ). Evidence from TDF in the Colombian Caribbean, such as in the Montes de María region, shows high levels of mortality for amphibians, reptiles, and mammals along peri-urban roads, with peaks related to seasonal scarcity of resources (De la Ossa-Nadjar and De la Ossa V 2013 ; 2015 ). In the Colombian Andes it was also shown that nocturnal species and specialized trophic guilds are particularly vulnerable in peri-urban areas with remaining forest cover (Obando-Tobón et al. 2024 ). results.header: Biodiversity and urban low-carbon development: an empirical study from Haidian District, Beijing | Urban Ecosystems | Springer Nature Link Skip to main content Advertisement Log in Menu Find a journal Publish with us Track your research Search Saved research Cart Home Urban Ecosystems Article Biodiversity and urban low-carbon development: an empirical study from Haidian District, Beijing Research Open access Published: 28 October 2026 Volume 29 , article number 301 ( 2026 ) Cite this article You have full access to this open access article Download PDF Save article View saved research Urban Ecosystems Aims and scope Submit manuscript Biodiversity and urban low-carbon development: an empirical study from Haidian District, Beijing Download PDF Wei Dai 1 , Yukun Zhang 2 & Tim Heath 3 218 Accesses Explore all metrics Abstract Urban areas face the dual challenge of mitigating carbon emissions while halting biodiversity loss, yet longitudinal evidence from Asian megacities on whether biodiversity independently enhances carbon sequestration remains limited. This study examines the biodiversity–carbon relationship using a twelve-year panel dataset from Haidian District, Beijing—a highly urbanized region where green space expansion has largely reached its spatial limits. Based on a systematic monitoring network of 40 permanent quadrats across 22 subdistricts, we constructed a comprehensive Biodiversity Index (BD) integrating plant, bird, amphibian, and soil fauna diversity with ecosystem quality and ecological function indicators. Using Generalized Linear Mixed Models (GLMMs) with quadrat and year as random effects, we find that the BD index is positively associated with carbon sink capacity, whereas green coverage alone does not. Plant and bird diversity emerge as positive predictors, with amphibian diversity exhibiting context-dependent effects confined to wetland habitats. The increasing marginal contribution of biodiversity to carbon sinks over time is consistent with a "quality transition" from area-based to quality-driven greening. The findings provide longitudinal empirical evidence that biodiversity restoration is associated with low-carbon development after urbanization stabilizes. Policy implications include integrating biodiversity premiums into carbon accounting, prioritizing functional complementarity in species selection, and protecting ecological corridors that sustain trophic interactions. Environmental Geography Environmental Economics Biodiversity Environmental Studies Urban Ecology Environmental Impact Urban Biodiversity and Ecosystem Management Introduction The accelerating pace of global urbanization has placed cities at the epicenter of both the climate crisis and the biodiversity extinction crisis. Urban areas currently account for approximately 70% of global CO 2 emissions while simultaneously experiencing some of the most rapid rates of habitat loss and species decline (Seto et al. 2012 ; Grimm et al. 2008 ). This dual burden has catalyzed urgent calls for urban development pathways that simultaneously mitigate carbon emissions and reverse biodiversity loss—a paradigm increasingly framed under the umbrella of nature-based solutions (Cohen-Shacham et al. 2019 ; Chausson et al. 2020 ). Yet a persistent tension haunts the relationship between urban conservation and climate action. Traditional urban planning has often treated biodiversity protection and carbon mitigation as competing priorities, with green space allocation driven primarily by area-based targets rather than ecological quality metrics (Lepczyk et al. 2017 ; Aronson et al. 2017 ). This "quantity over quality" approach has produced a troubling pattern: cities worldwide have expanded their green infrastructure coverage while simultaneously experiencing biotic homogenization—the gradual replacement of diverse native species assemblages with a handful of cosmopolitan, disturbance-tolerant species that contribute far less to ecosystem functioning (McKinney 2006 ; Clavel et al. 2011 ). The fundamental question, therefore, is not whether urban greening matters for climate mitigation—the answer is unequivocally yes—but rather: Does biodiversity itself, as a measure of ecological quality beyond simple vegetation cover, associate with enhance urban carbon sequestration capacity? Białas ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-0683-4001 1 & … Łukasz Dylewski ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-1370-7625 1 Show authors 301 Accesses Explore all metrics Summary Urbanization is a pervasive driver of habitat transformation, yet its effects on the taxonomic and functional structure of pollinator communities remain insufficiently resolved. We sampled bees and hoverflies along a semi-natural–suburban–urban gradient in the Poznań city to examine how urbanization influences taxonomic and functional community structure and patterns of beta diversity differ between pollinator taxa. Semi-natural habitats supported the highest bee and hoverfly abundances and species richness and, for bees, the greatest alpha diversity, indicating strong negative impacts on diversity of local assemblages. Nonmetric multidimensional scaling revealed significant shifts in community composition for both groups, with hoverfly communities showing stronger separation among urbanization levels than bee communities, suggesting greater sensitivity of hoverflies to urban environmental change. Functional responses differed between taxa: in bees, functional dispersion declined in urban sites, indicating trait clustering and environmental filtering, whereas in hoverflies, functional richness was markedly reduced in suburban and urban habitats, pointing to the loss of larval and adult trait diversity. Partitioning of beta diversity revealed taxon-specific patterns in both taxonomic and functional dimensions. Overall, our findings show that urbanization restructures pollinator communities through taxonomic and functional reorganization, with responses differing between bees and hoverflies. The observed beta diversity patterns suggest that urbanization is associated with taxon-specific patterns of differentiation. Because our study is based on one city in Poland, caution is warranted when extrapolating these results to other urban systems. Maintaining a mosaic of semi-natural, suburban, and urban green spaces that provides diverse floral resources, nesting substrates, and larval microhabitats will be essential to conserve pollinator diversity in increasingly urban landscapes. Biodiversity Entomology Urban Ecology Ecology Urban Sociology Ecosystems Urban Pollinator Ecology and Conservation Introduction Human-induced changes to landscapes play a pivotal role in the substantial loss and fragmentation of natural habitats (McKinney 2002 ; Grimm et al. 2008 ). This transformation has far-reaching implications for both biodiversity and the functioning of ecosystems (Fischer and Lindenmayer 2007 ; Cardinale et al. 2012 ). The global-scale conversion of natural habitats into urban or agricultural landscapes by human activities has been widespread (Seto et al. 2011 ), leading to shifts in patterns of species diversity and the provision of ecosystem services (Dirzo et al. 2014 ). Pollinating insects have emerged as a flagship group for raising public awareness of the impacts of human activities on biodiversity (Fortel et al. 2014 ). Pollinators play a vital role in maintaining the balance of ecosystems by facilitating the reproduction of flowering plants through the transfer of pollen. results.header: Green-roof ecosystem-service assessments under varying water-supply regimes: an evidence map of scope, gaps and research priorities | Urban Ecosystems | Springer Nature Link Skip to main content Advertisement Log in Menu Find a journal Publish with us Track your research Search Saved research Cart Home Urban Ecosystems Article Green-roof ecosystem-service assessments under varying water-supply regimes: an evidence map of scope, gaps and research priorities Review Published: 28 October 2026 Volume 29 , article number 299 ( 2026 ) Cite this article Save article View saved research Urban Ecosystems Aims and scope Submit manuscript Pius Otwil 1 , 2 , Zhikun Li 1 , Tonghui Yang 1 , Jing Wei 3 , 4 , Zetong Niu 1 , Ao Wang 5 , Muhammad Junaid Nazir 1 & … Longfei Yu ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-2127-6343 1 , 2 Show authors 26 Accesses Explore all metrics Abstract Vegetated green roofs (VGRs) provide multiple urban ecosystem benefits, including cooling, stormwater management, biodiversity support, and carbon-related ecosystem services. However, sustaining these benefits under increasing water scarcity and heat exposure remains challenging. Although experimental research on VGR plant and substrate responses to water limitation is expanding, variation in water-supply regimes, experimental scale, duration, and outcome measures may limit the comparability and generalisability of existing evidence, underscoring the need for a structured assessment of its scope and limitations. Accordingly, we combined a bibliometric analysis of 943 Scopus-indexed articles (2005–2025) with a structured synthesis of 161 empirical studies to map evidence across water-supply regimes, experimental settings, heat-exposure designs, and ecosystem services. We found uneven geographical coverage, with research concentrated in a few cities and established institutional sites, several of which supported long-term research and multiple publications. Although 68 studies examined heat exposure alongside water limitation, two imposed warming under water-limited conditions, and interpretation was constrained by limitations in treatment comparisons, measurement timing, sensor reliability, correlated predictor variables, and changes in irrigation practices. We identified major evidence gaps concerning links between plant responses and the maintenance or recovery of VGR ecosystem services, across cooling, habitat and biodiversity, stormwater regulation, and carbon regulation. Key priorities to address these gaps are proposed, centred on linking plant responses to service outcomes over the same drying and recovery periods, improving comparability across studies, and broadening the roof environments represented. These priorities may guide future work on VGR design and management under water-limited conditions. Highlights Thematic analysis of 943 articles and empirical evidence mapping of 161 studies revealed differences between thematic emphasis and empirical evidence coverage. Evidence linking plant responses to the maintenance and recovery of VGR ecosystem-service provision remains limited. Only two included studies imposed warming under water-limited conditions; evidence on interactions between warming and water-limited conditions remained limited. Research coverage was uneven across regions, with studies also concentrated in a few cities and experimental sites.
